newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - Bosnian refugees fear deportation from Germany.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Bosnian refugees fear deportation from Germany.

text.p: When the Balkan war advanced towards her Bosnian village in 1993, Adina Zlovic and her family fled the advancing Croatian army and arrived in Germany shaken by the massacres that she had only barely escaped.
Three years later, Zlovic will soon be on the run again.
The Germany that welcomed her in late 1993 will soon ask her to leave. Cash-strapped German states say they can no longer afford to support 400,000 refugees from former Yugoslavia.
A Moslem woman married to a Croat army deserter, Zlovic fled with her infant daughter just before her home town of Vares was overrun by Croat soldiers and hundreds of Moslems were slaughtered.
Zlovic, a dark-haired 32-year-old Arabic scholar, says there is no future in ethnically divided Bosnia for such multi-cultural families like hers.

"There's nothing worse than being a refugee," Zlovic said. "No one wants us. We can't go back to Bosnia because I am Moslem and my husband is Croat. We have no home there any more. If Germany throws us out, we will have nothing."
FEAR HAUNTS REFUGEES AS DEPORTATION NEARS
Zlovic, along with thousands of Moslem, Serb, and Croat refugees will be forced to leave Germany when the pace of involuntary repatriation quickens once the winter ends.
Anxiety is spreading through the refugee community in Berlin as the dreaded hour approaches. The forced deportations could begin in April or sooner.

One distraught refugee facing deportation in December killed himself and another hijacked a plane in desperation, putting a kitchen knife to the throat of the pilot and forcing an Austrian Airlines aircraft bound for Vienna to return to Berlin, where he was overwhelmed by police and arrested.
"There is much despair among the refugees," said Annelore Hermes from the Society for Threatened Peoples, a lobby group that works closely with Bosnian refugees.
"Their worst fears about the conditions in Bosnia are justified. There is a lot of tension and resistance."
GERMANY'S WELCOME FOR REFUGEES WEARS THIN

During the 3-1/2 year Balkan war, Germany took in more refugees than the rest of the European Union combined. Haunted by its own memories of war and its aftermath, Germany welcomed refugees with enthusiasm, providing shelter and about 1,000 marks ($610) per family per month in spending money, cash that many stashed away and sent to relatives who stayed in Bosnia.

But after the fighting stopped in 1995, the welcoming arms quickly grew weary. German states paying for the refugees were disappointed that only a small trickle left. It costs Berlin about 500 million marks ($300 million) a year to support 30,000 refugees.

The frustration reached a peak last October when the states in Europe's richest country said they would start forcing the refugees to leave. The United Nations UNHCR refugee agency criticised the move and NATO said the issue of returning refugees was so explosive it could undermine the peace process.

So far only two dozen have been bundled off -- and many of those were convicted criminals. But after waiting for the winter to end, Germany plans to send 90,000 home by July 1 -- all the single adults and married children.
Those remaining -- the families with children -- will be ordered to leave starting in mid-1997.
REFUGEES SPEAK OF DANGERS OF RETURNING HOME

Many refugees say they would like nothing more than to return home. But their homes have been destroyed or occupied by displaced persons from other parts of former Yugoslavia, who were given priority over those who fled abroad.
Many refugees are Moslems whose home towns are now under Croat or Serb control.

"Where am I supposed to go?" said Fahrulin Sehovic, a 56-year-old Bosnian Moslem who fled with his wife and two sons to Berlin in 1993. His family-owned printing business and house in Capljina near Mostar have since been expropriated by Croats.

"Bosnia is still a very dangerous place for us," said Sehovic, who went for weeks with little or no food in Serb detention camps. His weight fell by 20 kg (44 lbs) to 55 kg before he escaped and fled to Berlin.
"We are afraid of beatings, torture and discrimination."
Sehovic's permit in Berlin expires in April. He is especially worried about the fate of his two draft-age sons -- 22 and 20 years old.
"If we go back I am afraid they will be arrested," he said. "Those who don't want to go back should not be forced out."
PUNISHMENT, DISCRIMINATION AWAITS RETURNEES, REFUGEES SAY

Many of the refugees who evaded the draft or deserted are most fearful of the looming repatriation because they expect punishment upon their return -- even though such retribution was supposedly ruled out by the Dayton peace agreement.

Satko Selimovic, a 27-year-old Moslem who fought in the Bosnian army for four years, said he doesn't want to return because of the lingering animosity. Even though he was injured by a Serb grenade attack, his best friend in Berlin is a Serb.
"I don't want to live in a place where this is so much hatred," he said. "People I don't even know hate me. It is awful. I can't go back."
Others fear being ostracised by those who stayed behind for spending the war in relative luxury in wealthy Germany.

"Once people down in Bosnia find out you were in Germany during the war years you have problems," said Eugen Duvnjak, a 23-year-old studying to become a teacher. "There is a lot of discrimination against those in Germany. They think everyone earned a fortune here, while they were fighting and suffering."
REFUGEES DRIVEN TO SUICIDE
Most of the refugees in Berlin fear the fires of religious intolerance that started the war in the first place.

Zlovic, the Arabic language scholar, said that apart from fears of the uncharted minefields, the main reason she will not return to Bosnia is the intolerance towards her mixed marriage and especially her five-year-old daughter.

"It didn't matter before what religion you were," she said. "Now, it is no longer important who I am but instead what my name is. You have to belong to a religion now. You have to be Catholic or Moslem. No one wants people with mixed marriages."

Zlovic said she expected there would be more suicides in the months ahead like that of Senad Becirovic, a 34-year-Bosnian Moslem who killed himself in November. He was about to be repatriated and his home was under Serb control.
"There will be many more," she said. "It is psychological terror to be forced back. They only see into this tunnel and have no idea what will happen to them. They see no way out." ($1=1.6413 Mark)
